body.text: On September 14, while addressing a Gen Z Mahajutan or public meeting in Gorakhpur, Neha Bora, a PhD scholar at Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) and national president of the All India Students’ Association (AISA), described the Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Adityanath as a “goonda” and a “dangai” (rioter), among other things. She accused him of turning Gorakhpur—once associated with Buddha and Kabir—into “a land of riots” and of presiding over paper leaks, unemployment, and the persecution of minorities and Dalits through bulldozer demolitions. “What education can he give Uttar Pradesh?" she challenged.

As expected, the response was immediate and disproportionate to the offence, if it was an offence. Three police complaints were filed against her; BJP functionaries demanded an FIR; and Minister Om Prakash Rajbhar publicly threatened her with the “right medicine” for what he called her “theatrics”. This followed a pattern already visible in Neha’s activism elsewhere—she has been targeted online with what commentators have described as a torrent of hate campaigns. Earlier, during the Jharkhand agitation, a BJP-backed activist had thrown ink at her while calling her “anti-national”. AISA reportedly received several messages and voice notes threatening death to Neha; they filed a complaint along with evidence to the Uttar Pradesh Director General of Police (DGP) on September 15, 2026.

Objectively speaking, Neha is well within her constitutional rights, stating facts about a public functionary that are in the public record. It is rather the threats and intimidatory responses from Adityanath’s ministers that constitute a far graver breach of democratic norms than the language Neha used. The charges that she levelled against Adityanath have a documented relationship to episodes in his own political record.

After he became Chief Minister, Adityanath’s government ordered the withdrawal of a 1995 criminal case against him and many others for violating prohibitory orders. The withdrawal was pursued under a statutory procedure requiring the public prosecutor to apply to the court. It was not unprecedented; earlier, the Samajwadi Party in the State also had done it. But it was surely amoral that the state government exercised its power to withdraw cases where the sitting Chief Minister himself was an accused. Subsequently, the government went on to promote legislation aimed at withdrawing or abating the thousands of pending cases that involved political leaders.
The constitutional position

Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression, and the Supreme Court has consistently recognised criticism of the government and public functionaries as central to that freedom. Political speech directed at those exercising public power lies at the heart of Article 19(1)(a). The restrictions permitted under Article 19(2)—including defamation, public order, decency or morality, and incitement to an offence—do not make harsh or unflattering criticism a crime merely because it embarrasses those in power.

Indian defamation law itself distinguishes criticism of public conduct from private insult. The exceptions to Section 499 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), now carried into the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, protect true imputations made for the public good and opinions expressed in good faith on the public conduct of public servants. In S. Khushboo v. Kanniammal (2010), the Supreme Court stressed that a free society must tolerate even unpopular and dissenting views, while Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016), although upholding criminal defamation, recognised the protection accorded to fair criticism of public functionaries in their public capacity. The criticism of the exercise of public power cannot be equated with a private insult.

The reason is obvious. A Chief Minister who controls the police, administration, and prosecution is not similarly situated to a private citizen. Public power must remain open to public scrutiny, including sharp and uncomfortable criticism. Otherwise, the citizen’s right to hold power accountable becomes meaningless. In the present case, the filing of police complaints and threatening responses by ministers against a young activist make this distinction particularly important.

The question is not whether Neha’s language was intemperate, but whether criticism of those who exercise state power can be answered through the coercive machinery of the state. The alleged intemperance of language in this case stems from the language of dissent. It cannot be judged as though it were exchanged between political equals. The very fact that the criticism caught on with people as well as in the corridors of power establishes its appropriateness.
What about constitutional morality

What makes the controversy unusual is that Neha’s charges correspond closely to Adityanath’s own documented criminal record. His 2017 election affidavit disclosed pending cases involving rioting (Section 147, IPC), defiling a place of worship (Section 295), trespass on burial grounds (Section 297), mischief by fire or explosives (Section 436), criminal intimidation (Section 506), and disobedience of a public order (Section 188). The affidavit records no conviction.

A separate case arose from a 1995 meeting in Pipiganj, when Adityanath and others were booked under Section 188 for holding a meeting despite prohibitory orders. After becoming Chief Minister, Adityanath’s government ordered the prosecution to seek withdrawal of the case. A 2007 case arising from communal violence in Gorakhpur also named him as an accused. The investigation initially led to charges under Sections 147, 295, 297, 436, and 506, while Section 153A, concerning promotion of enmity between groups, was subsequently added after the required sanction was obtained. His earlier 2014 election affidavit also disclosed a separate case involving Section 307 (attempt to murder), along with Sections 147, 148, 149, 336, 504, and 427.

In 2017, Adityanath’s government initiated the withdrawal of thousands of cases, describing them as politically motivated. The first tranche included a case against himself as well as cases against Keshav Prasad Maurya and Shiv Pratap Shukla. And, in his 2022 election affidavit, Adityanath declared that there were no pending criminal cases against him.

Neha’s description of Adityanath thus cannot be dismissed as baseless. The striking feature of the episode is that her language has attracted intense scrutiny, while the far more consequential question—the misuse of power by a Chief Minister in withdrawing criminal proceedings against himself—has received comparatively less attention.
Political environment and vocabulary

Neha’s language also needs to be viewed against Adityanath’s own political rhetoric as Chief Minister. His public discourse has repeatedly employed the language of force, punishment, and retribution. Soon after assuming office, he said that criminals would be gunned down, “thok diye jayenge”; in his 2022 election campaign, he warned that the “garmi” (heat) of those associated with riots and crime would be “cooled down” after the election; in the Assembly in 2023, following the murder of Umesh Pal, he declared that the “mafia” would be reduced to dust, “mitti mein mila denge”.

The Adityanath government’s encounter policy subsequently became a prominent feature of its claim to tough governance. Alongside the rhetoric of summary physical punishment, Adityanath has made recurrent use of religiously polarising language. His “80:20” formulation during the 2022 election campaign, the “abba jaan” remark, and his repeated references to riots, Pakistan, and “infiltrators” have been documented by independent monitors as part of a broader pattern of anti-Muslim or religiously polarising political speech. Monitoring organisations have recorded dozens of speeches made by Adityanath during the 2024 election campaign that were classified as hate speech, their counts differing as per methodology.

This is the political environment in which Neha made her speech. An environment shaped by a vocabulary of force, punishment, religious polarisation, and the assertion of overwhelming state power. Neha’s description of Adityanath as a “goonda” or “rioter” did not arise in a political vacuum. When those in power reserve for themselves the foul language of force and intimidation, they cannot reasonably demand from those who challenge them a language of polite deference.

BJP leaders and their supporters would respond that withdrawn cases are not proof of guilt, that many were genuinely stale or filed with political intent by earlier governments. It is also true that successive Uttar Pradesh governments, including that of the Samajwadi Party, have withdrawn cases against their leaders. Citing unproven charges as settled fact rather than as “alleged” appears to cross from fair commentary to defamatory assertion, and ordinarily that would be correct. Unfortunately, this is not an ordinary instance. The cases were not dismissed through judicial process. They were withdrawn by the government the accused now leads. Given this, how can people express disapproval of Adityanath other than by relying on public record? During her speech, Neha Bora represented the people, committed to the constitutional promise that citizens may hold power to account without fearing it.

A democracy that is secure in its institutions does not need to weaponise the police against a student activist for saying, in blunt language, what its own official records already show. Neha’s characterisation of Adityanath rests on a documented history of criminal charges that his government chose to extinguish rather than contest in court, a fact that deserves closer scrutiny than Neha’s choice of words. The Constitution’s guarantee of free speech was written precisely for moments like this one, and Neha deserves commendation from the people of India for saying on their behalf what they themselves could not, out of fear, state out loud.
Anand Teltumbde is a civil rights activist and the author of over 30 books. He is the former CEO of Petronet India Ltd and a professor at IIT Kharagpur and the Goa Institute of Management
